papers.title_in_file: Deep-Q Learning with Hybrid Quantum Neural Network on Solving Maze Problems
papers.what_it_is: A hybrid classical-quantum deep Q-learning agent (CNN plus a two-qubit Qiskit Sampler-QNN layer) trained on 4x4 and 5x5 maze problems in a noise-free simulator.

assertions.value: The authors report that on a 4x4 maze the classical CNN had 6588 parameters, a 89.94% win rate and an 88.29 sec training runtime, while the hybrid QNN had 2442 parameters, an 85.19% win rate and a 700.28 sec runtime. On a 5x5 maze the classical CNN had 7114 parameters, 94.87% and 297.86 sec, and the hybrid QNN had 4890 parameters, 93.13% and 1577.37 sec.
assertions.anchor: Section V.B, Tables II and III, p.6
quotes: Classical CNN 6588 89.94% 88.29 sec
Hybrid QNN 2442 85.19% 700.28 sec
Classical CNN 7114 94.87% 297.86 sec
Hybrid QNN 4890 93.13% 1577.37 sec
COMPARISON OF MODEL PERFORMANCES ON 4X4 MAZE SIZE
COMPARISON OF MODEL PERFORMANCES ON 5X5 MAZE SIZE
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study; rows of Tables II and III (4x4 and 5x5 maze), p.6.
assertions.reader_inference: In the paper's own tables the hybrid model has fewer parameters (about 2442 against 6588 on 4x4) but a lower win rate and a much longer runtime (700.28 sec against 88.29 sec on 4x4). The tables show no parameter-efficiency advantage that translates into better performance. No repeated runs or variance are reported.

assertions.value: The authors state that the quantum computation experiments were tested and trained on classical hardware with IBM Qiskit's Aer simulator in an ideal, noise-free environment, and that training a hybrid model on a real quantum computer is challenging.
assertions.anchor: Abstract / Section I, p.1; Section VI.D Outlook, p.7
quotes: tested and trained on the full-classical hardware with IBM
ideal, noise-free environment
training a hybrid model on a real quantum computer is challenging
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of its experimental scope (Section I, p.1) and stated limit (Section VI.D, p.7).
assertions.reader_inference: No result in the paper tests the hybrid network on quantum hardware or under noise.

assertions.value: The authors state that some technical constraints remain in the hybrid architecture, such as quantum-classical gradient descent and accelerated computing devices for this model class.
assertions.anchor: Section VI.C Hybrid Neural Network, p.7
quotes: However, some technical constraints are still involved within this solution architecture
like quantum-classical gradient descent, accelerated computing devices for this model class, etc.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own stated limitation, Section VI.C, p.7.

papers.title_in_file: Efficient Quantum Recurrent Reinforcement Learning via Quantum Reservoir Computing
papers.what_it_is: A quantum A3C reinforcement learning agent whose QLSTM is randomly initialized and left untrained (a reservoir), tested in simulation on MiniGrid-Empty mazes.

assertions.value: The authors report from numerical simulation that the QLSTM reservoir RL framework reaches performance comparable to fully trained counterparts when the model sizes are the same and the training setting is the same.
assertions.anchor: Abstract and Section 7 Conclusions, p.1 and p.4
quotes: Our numerical simulation shows that the proposed framework can reach performance comparable to fully trained counterparts
shows stability and average scores comparable to their fully-trained counterparts in most testing cases
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study on MiniGrid-Empty; scores are shown in Figures 5 and 6 only.
assertions.reader_inference: The conclusion says comparable in most testing cases, not all. The numeric scores are in figures, not in the text.

assertions.value: The authors report that in the MiniGrid-8x8 case with a fixed starting point only the fully-trained QLSTM with 4 VQC layers reached the optimal performance, the QLSTM-RC with 2 VQC layers still learned but slowly, and other model configurations struggled to learn good policies.
assertions.anchor: Section 6.4 Results, MiniGrid with fixed starting point, p.3
quotes: In the most difficult MiniGrid-8x8 case, only the fully-trained QLSTM with 4 VQC layers reaches the optimal performance.
The QLSTM-RC with 2 VQC layers still learns but slowly.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study; the evidence is a learning curve in Figure 5.
assertions.reader_inference: On the hardest tested environment the untrained reservoir did not match the fully trained model, which qualifies the comparable-performance claim.

assertions.value: The authors state that the hybrid models use an 8-qubit VQC-based QLSTM with input and hidden dimensions of 4, explore 1, 2 and 4 VQC layers, and train with 80 parallel local agents using asynchronous advantage actor-critic on the MiniGrid-Empty environment.
quotes: we utilize an 8-qubit VQC-based QLSTM model with input and hidden dimensions of 4.
We explore QLSTM variations with 1, 2, and 4 VQC layers
The number of parallel processes (local agents) is 80.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup, Sections 6.2 and 6.3, p.3.
assertions.reader_inference: All results come from simulation on a maze task; no hardware run is reported.

papers.title_in_file: Quantum deep Q learning with distributed prioritized experience replay
papers.what_it_is: A quantum DQN framework (QDQN-DPER) with asynchronous training, prioritized experience replay and a modified matrix loss, simulated on a modified Cart-Pole task.

assertions.value: The authors report that in all CartPoleMod settings quantum models with prioritized experience replay beat classical models of similar size and architecture, and that the model with both prioritized experience replay and matrix loss consistently outperformed the other quantum models.
assertions.anchor: Section 6.3 Results, p.7-9 (scores are in Figure 3 only)
quotes: quantum models with prioritized experience replay beat the classical models with similar model size (number of parameters) and architecture
the model equipped with both prioritized experience replay and matrix loss consistently outperformed the other two quantum models
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study; the scores appear only in Figure 3.
assertions.reader_inference: No numeric scores, repeated-run counts or significance tests are given in the text.

assertions.value: The authors state that the evaluation uses simulation on the CartPoleMod environment with versions v0 (no noise), v1 and v2 (5% and 10% uniform actuator noise) and v3 (5% uniform sensor noise), 50,000 episodes per setting, and an 8-qubit VQC with 48 quantum parameters.
quotes: v0 represents an environment without any noise, whereas v1 and v2 introduce 5% and 10% uniform actuator noise
v3 incorporates 5% uniform sensor noise
We perform simulation for each environment and setting with 50,000 episodes.
namely 8, and two variational layers have been incorporated into its design
the VQC employs a total of 48 quantum parameters
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup, Sections 6.1 and 6.2, p.7.

assertions.value: The authors state that the superior performance is shown against traditional quantum deep Q-network models that lack the prioritized replay memory or the modified loss function, in the benchmark tasks considered.
quotes: superior performance compared to traditional quantum deep Q-network models that lack the prioritized replay memory or modified loss function in the benchmark tasks considered
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of the scope of its comparison, Section 7, p.9.
assertions.reader_inference: The tested tasks are variants of one environment (Cart-Pole). The classical comparison models are matched in architecture and size to the quantum model, and the paper reports no comparison with other well-tuned classical RL agents.

papers.title_in_file: An Introduction to Quantum Reinforcement Learning (QRL)
papers.what_it_is: A short introductory survey of variational-circuit-based quantum reinforcement learning (quantum Q-learning, policy gradients, recurrent policies, fast weight programmers, architecture search).

assertions.value: The paper defines quantum reinforcement learning (QRL) as the use of quantum neural networks for learning policy or value functions.
quotes: The use of quantum neural networks for learning policy or value functions is referred to as quantum reinforcement learning (QRL).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own definition of the term, Section III.A, p.2.

assertions.value: The paper states, citing earlier work, that a QLSTM reservoir can achieve performance comparable to fully trained models even without training, and that numerical simulations showed a randomly initialized QLSTM reservoir RL agent comparable to, and sometimes superior to, fully trained QLSTM RL agents.
quotes: It has been shown that even without training, the QLSTM reservoir can achieve performance comparable to fully trained models [8].
the QLSTM reservoir can achieve performance comparable to, and sometimes superior to, fully trained QLSTM RL agents
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the survey attributes to other work (references [8] and [19]), not shown in this paper.
assertions.reader_inference: The cited work is by the same author, and the survey gives no numbers.

assertions.value: The paper states, citing reference [31], that the authors of that work extended the A3C framework to quantum settings and showed that VQC actors and critics can outperform classical models when the model sizes are comparable.
quotes: In [31], the authors extend the A3C framework to quantum settings, showing that VQC actors and critics can outperform classical models when the sizes of the models are comparable.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result attributed to a cited work, Section III.C, p.3.

assertions.value: The paper states that in the NISQ era a major challenge for QML applications is the limited quantum resources, which complicates both the training and inference phases, and that trainability challenges in QRL models are a topic for future research.
quotes: a major challenge for QML applications is the limited quantum resources, which complicates both the training and inference phases
Future research could further explore the trainability challenges in QRL models
assertions.certainty_reason: A general statement about the state of the field with no study behind it, Section IV, p.4.

papers.title_in_file: Noise-Aware Distributed Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm on Near-term Quantum Hardware
papers.what_it_is: A framework that splits large QAOA problems into subproblems, filters qubits and gates by error threshold, and spreads sampling across several QPUs, benchmarked with the HamilToniQ H-Score.

assertions.value: The authors state that they used five QPUs as nodes to accomplish six samplings for a 6-qubit QAOA problem, where ibm guadalupe with 16 qubits can hold two sampling zones on one chip, and that a 15-qubit QAOA problem was decomposed into smaller problems of 4, 5 and 6 qubits with the Balanced MinCut method.
assertions.anchor: Section V.A and V.B, p.4-5 (H-Score values are in Figures 4 and 5 only)
quotes: We utilize five QPUs as nodes to accomplish six samplings for a 6-qubit QAOA problem (where ibm guadalupe, with 16 qubits, can accommodate two sampling zones on a single chip).
We demonstrate this by addressing a 15-qubit QAOA problem, which can be decomposed into smaller QAOA problems of 4, 5, and 6 qubits using the Balanced MinCut method
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own experimental setup, Section V.A and V.B.
assertions.reader_inference: The text gives no H-Score numbers. The outcome appears only in figures.

assertions.value: The authors claim that their proof-of-concept simulations demonstrated the potential of the framework for large QAOA algorithms and compared it with a naive QAOA strategy, and that using HamilToniQ as a resource management toolkit significantly enhances the accuracy of large-scale QAOA algorithms.
assertions.anchor: Section V.B and Section VI Conclusion, p.5
quotes: Our proof-of-concept simulations have demonstrated the potential of the proposed framework
The use of HamilToniQ as a resource management toolkit significantly enhances the accuracy of large-scale QAOA algorithms by efficiently allocating computational resources.
assertions.certainty_reason: An author claim; the text gives no numbers, and the supporting data are in figures.
assertions.reader_inference: The abstract also claims significant improvements in computational speed and accuracy. The text reports no speed or accuracy figures, and no real-hardware run is described in the text read.

assertions.value: The authors state that the threshold filtering step has complexity O(N + E), where N is the number of qubits and E the number of edges, and that the fidelity calculation for potential qubit blocks has complexity O(N log N).
quotes: exhibits a complexity of O(N + E), where N represents the number of qubits and E represents the number of edges
has a complexity of O(N log N )
assertions.certainty_reason: Stated without derivation, Section IV.C.1.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper asserts these costs without a proof or a measured run time.

assertions.value: The authors state that the core concept of distributed QAOA is to disregard nodes with low-fidelity qubits and high two-qubit gate errors (greater than 0.01), then decompose the QAOA problem into smaller subproblems compiled onto high-fidelity qubits.
quotes: The core concept of distributed QAOA involves disregarding nodes characterized by low-fidelity qubits and high two-qubit gate errors (greater than 0.01).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own method, Section III.

papers.title_in_file: A Novel Image Classification Framework Based on Variational Quantum Algorithms
papers.version_note: The file is in the 2023 folder; it is arXiv 2312.07932v2 dated 6 Mar 2024. The title and content match the record.
papers.what_it_is: An image classification framework that replaces global pooling after a ResNet-18 or MaxViT-T backbone with an amplitude-encoded variational quantum circuit, simulated on four public datasets.

assertions.value: The authors report from simulated experiments on four public datasets that MaxViT-T_q gave up to 9.21% higher accuracy and up to 15.79% higher F1 score than MaxViT-T, and that ResNet-18_q gave up to 5.70% higher test accuracy and up to 5.53% higher test F1 score than ResNet-18.
quotes: More remarkably, MaxViT-T q provides up to 9.21% higher accuracy and up to 15.79% higher F1 score, when compared with MaxViT.
ResNet-18 q exhibits improvements in test accuracy of up to 5.70% and in test F1 score of up to 5.53%, over the classical ResNet-18 model.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study (Tables 3 and 4), simulator only.
assertions.reader_inference: Tables 3 and 4 give single values with no variance or repeated runs. The models are trained from scratch on small datasets, and some absolute accuracies are low (for example the Aircraft subset). The classical baseline keeps the same backbone with global pooling, so the comparison mixes pooling removal with the added circuit.

assertions.value: The authors report that MaxViT-T_q achieved better classification performance than MaxViT-T on the BUSI and AOT datasets using only 0.2% and 0.4% of the number of parameters, and state that only the parameters of the layers after the backbone are counted.
quotes: MaxViT-T q achieves better classification performances than MaxViT-T on BUSI and AOT Datasets, using only 0.2% and 0.4% of the number of parameters, respectively
we only present the parameter count of the layers after the backbone model
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study (Table 4).
assertions.reader_inference: The parameter comparison excludes the shared backbone, so the reduction applies to the head only, not to the whole model.

assertions.value: The authors state that with amplitude encoding a ResNet-18 feature map of 25088 values needs only 15 qubits, whereas angle encoding would need 25088 qubits.
quotes: = 15 qubits are needed to encode those feature maps.
25088 qubits required by angle encoding for the case of ResNet-18
assertions.certainty_reason: A direct consequence of the amplitude encoding definition the paper uses, Section 2.4.
assertions.reader_inference: The paper does not discuss the cost of preparing an amplitude-encoded state on hardware.

assertions.value: The authors state as limitations that only two ansatzes were used, that all experiments were done with quantum simulators and not real quantum hardware, and that the method was investigated only for image classification.
quotes: Secondly, we perform all experiments with quantum simulators in this work.
Thirdly, we investigate our method only in the area of image classification.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own stated limits, Section 4, p.6.

papers.title_in_file: Learning to Learn with Quantum Optimization via Quantum Neural Networks
papers.what_it_is: A meta-learning scheme in which a QLSTM acts as the optimizer of QAOA parameters, trained on 7-node Max-Cut graphs and tested on larger Max-Cut and Sherrington-Kirkpatrick instances in simulation.

assertions.value: The authors report, for the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model at iteration 3 with p = 1, that both QLSTM and LSTM optimizers give approximation ratios near unity for system sizes from 8 to 16 nodes, while Adam and Adagrad start around 0.42 for 8 nodes and reach approximately 0.58 by 16 nodes.
quotes: Table II presents the approximation ratios at iteration 3 for p = 1 across various optimizers applied to the SK model.
both QLSTM and LSTM consistently yield ratios near unity across system sizes ranging from 8 to 16 nodes
Adam and Adagrad starting around 0.42 for 8 nodes and only reaching approximately 0.58 by 16 nodes
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical simulation result from one study (Table II).
assertions.reader_inference: Table II also lists SGD at 0.92 to 0.96 for 11 to 16 nodes and R-QAOA at 0.83 to 0.93, so the text statement that classical optimizers have significantly lower ratios holds for Adam, Adagrad and RMSProp but not for every baseline. Each run is one iteration-3 value with no spread shown.

assertions.value: The authors state that at lower connectivity (P = 2/7) the QLSTM optimizer exhibits the highest approximation ratio on Max-Cut instances, which they generated as random Erdos-Renyi graphs with twenty instances per setting.
quotes: Notably, at lower connectivity (e.g., P = 2/7), QLSTM exhibits the highest approximation ratio
We generated twenty such random instances for each pair
assertions.certainty_reason: An author statement about Table I; it is not consistent with the table's own R-QAOA row.
assertions.reader_inference: Table I lists R-QAOA at 0.92 and QLSTM at 0.82 for P = 2/7, so the table does not support the claim that QLSTM is highest at that setting. The text also says iteration 2 in one place and iteration 3 elsewhere, and it quotes 0.92 for QLSTM at P = 6/7 where the table lists 0.93. Treat this claim with caution.

assertions.value: The authors state that the QLSTM optimizer was trained on randomly generated Max-Cut instances with 7 nodes and evaluated on larger instances, and that training is performed in simulated quantum environments where gradients can be accurately estimated.
quotes: We have verified this transfer learning capability by training the QLSTM optimizer on randomly generated Max-Cut instances with N1 = 7 nodes
the training is performed using simulated quantum environments where gradients can be accurately estimated
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own training setup, Sections IV.D and IV.F.1.
assertions.reader_inference: All reported results are simulations, so noise on hardware is not tested.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing Bittel et al., that the classical training procedure central to variational quantum algorithms is itself NP-hard, which they describe as a fundamental limitation of VQA-based hybrid quantum computations.
quotes: recent work by Bittel et al. demonstrates that the classical training procedure central to variational quantum
highlighting a fundamental limitation in VQA-based hybrid quantum computations
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work (reference [15]).

papers.title_in_file: Learning to Measure Quantum Neural Networks
papers.what_it_is: A method that makes the measured observable (a parameterized Hermitian matrix) of a variational quantum circuit learnable, tested in simulation on make_moons and a 10-speaker speech task.

assertions.value: The authors report on a 10-speaker VCTK speaker recognition task that the VQC with fixed PauliZ measurement had final test accuracy 70.59%, the VQC with a learned Hermitian attained 76.83%, and giving different learning rates to the unitary gates and the Hermitian further reached 96.33%.
assertions.anchor: Section V.B.c Results and Fig. 7, p.4
quotes: the VQC with fixed PauliZ measurement (blue line) had accuracy 70.59%, while VQC of varying Hermitian (green line) attained 76.83%
Endowing different parameter learning rates to the unitary gates and the Hermitian (red line) further reached 96.33%.
to form the final speaker recognition dataset of 10 speakers (classes)
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study; simulation, 5 trials of 30 epochs.
assertions.reader_inference: The largest gain (to 96.33%) comes from a separate, larger learning rate for the Hermitian. This is a tuning change as well as a measurement change, and no classical-model baseline is reported for the task.

assertions.value: The authors report on make_moons data with noise levels 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 that the standard VQC without learnable observables had the lowest performance, and that the VQC with a learnable observable and a separate optimizer outperformed the VQC with a learnable observable alone.
assertions.anchor: Section V.A Task 1, Figures 3 to 5, p.3
quotes: The dataset is generated with noise levels of 0.1, 0.2, and 0.3.
The standard VQC model without learnable observables exhibits the lowest performance.
assertions.certainty_reason: Empirical result from one study; the evidence is learning curves in Figures 3 to 5.
assertions.reader_inference: The text gives no numeric accuracies for this task. The outcome is a ranking read from figures.

assertions.value: The authors state that they parameterize the Hermitian matrix used as the observable and train its parameters concurrently with the standard quantum circuit rotation angles, and that each class adds 4 additional trainable parameters in the make_moons setup.
assertions.anchor: Section I p.1; Section V.A, p.3
quotes: we parameterize the Hermitian matrix used as observables and train these parameters concurrently with the standard quantum circuit parameters (rotation angles)
each class introduces 4 additional trainable parameters
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's statement of its own method and setup, Sections I and V.A.

assertions.value: The authors state that their results come from numerical simulations, and that using different parameter optimizers serves to demonstrate the concept while other optimization techniques for further improvement are possible.
quotes: Using numerical simulations, we show that the proposed method can identify observables
here using different parameter optimizers serves to demonstrate the concept
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of scope, Abstract and Section V.B.c.
assertions.reader_inference: No hardware or noise experiment is described.
